content: Estradiol (vaginal) is a hormone approved by the FDA for the treatment of vulvar and vaginal atrophy. It is important to note that this medication carries a Black Box Warning. Common adverse reactions include breast pain, upper respiratory tract infections, headaches, abdominal pain, general pain, and edema. The treatment should be limited to the shortest duration necessary to achieve treatment goals while minimizing risks for the individual patient. Periodic reevaluation, typically every 3 to 6 months, is recommended to assess the continued need for therapy. For the treatment of vulvar and vaginal atrophy associated with menopause, the lowest effective dose and regimen should be selected to control symptoms, and the medication should be discontinued as soon as possible. Women with a uterus should undergo appropriate diagnostic measures, such as endometrial sampling, to rule out malignancy in cases of unexplained persistent or recurrent abnormal vaginal bleeding. Attempts to discontinue or taper the medication should be made at 3to 6-month intervals. The usual dosage range is 2 to 4 grams daily for one or two weeks, followed by a gradual reduction to half the initial dosage for a similar period. A maintenance dosage of 1 gram, applied one to three times a week, may be used after the restoration of the vaginal mucosa. The number of doses per tube will vary depending on dosage requirements and patient handling. Off-label use of estradiol (vaginal) in adults and pediatric patients is not well-documented, and there is limited information regarding its safety and efficacy in these populations. Estradiol (vaginal) should not be used in women with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, known or suspected breast cancer, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, active or recent thromboembolic disorders, liver dysfunction or disease, known hypersensitivity to its ingredients, or known or suspected pregnancy. The use of estrogens has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism (VTE), and pulmonary embolism. If any of these events occur or are suspected, estrogens should be discontinued immediately. Risk factors for arterial vascular disease (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, smoking, hypercholesterolemia, obesity) and/or VTE (e.g., personal or family history of VTE, obesity, systemic lupus erythematosus) should be managed appropriately. In the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study, an increased risk of myocardial infarctions, strokes, and VTE was observed in women receiving conjugated estrogens (CE) with or without medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) compared to placebo. The use of unopposed estrogens in women with intact uteri has been associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer. The risk appears to be dependent on the duration of treatment and estrogen dose, with the greatest risk associated with prolonged use. Adding a progestin to estrogen therapy has been shown to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor to endometrial cancer. Estrogen and progestin therapy in postmenopausal women has also been reported to increase the risk of breast cancer, with the risk increasing with the duration of use. Observational studies suggest that the risk of breast cancer returns to baseline approximately five years after stopping treatment. In the Women’s Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS), postmenopausal women aged 65 years and older treated with conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate were reported to have a two-fold increase in the risk of developing probable dementia compared to placebo. It is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women or to estrogen-alone therapy. The use of estrogens has been associated with a 2to 4-fold increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery in postmenopausal women. Estrogen administration may also lead to severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases. If hypercalcemia occurs, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate measures should be taken to reduce serum calcium levels. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens. If sudden partial or complete loss of vision, proptosis, diplopia, or migraine occurs, the medication should be discontinued pending examination. If examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions, estrogens should be permanently discontinued. Other adverse reactions associated with estrogen and/or progestin therapy include changes in vaginal bleeding patterns, breakthrough bleeding, spotting, dysmenorrhea, increased size of uterine leiomyomata, vaginitis, genital pruritus, ovarian cancer, endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial cancer. Breast-related adverse effects include tenderness, enlargement, pain, nipple discharge, galactorrhea, and breast cancer. Cardiovascular effects include deep and superficial venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, thrombophlebitis, myocardial infarction, stroke, and increased blood pressure. Gastrointestinal effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, bloating, cholestatic jaundice, increased incidence of gallbladder disease, pancreatitis, and enlargement of hepatic hemangiomas. Skin-related effects include chloasma or melasma, erythema multiforme, erythema nodosum, hemorrhagic eruption, loss of scalp hair, hirsutism, pruritus, and rash. Central nervous system effects include headache, migraine, dizziness, mental depression, chorea, nervousness, mood disturbances, irritability, and exacerbation of epilepsy or dementia. Miscellaneous effects include weight changes, reduced carbohydrate tolerance, aggravation of porphyria, edema, arthralgias, leg cramps, changes in libido, urticaria, angioedema, hypersensitivity reactions, hypocalcemia, exacerbation of asthma, and increased triglycerides. Estradiol (vaginal) should only be administered to pediatric patients when clearly indicated, and the lowest effective dose should always be used. Large and repeated doses of estrogen in prepubertal children may accelerate epiphyseal closure, resulting in short adult stature. Periodic monitoring of bone maturation and effects on epiphyseal centers is recommended in patients whose bone growth is not complete. Estrogen treatment in prepubertal children may also induce premature breast development, vaginal cornification, and vaginal bleeding in girls, and may modify the normal pubertal process in boys. In geriatric patients, the use of conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate has been associated with a two-fold increase in the risk of developing probable dementia. Alzheimer’s disease was the most common classification of probable dementia in both the treatment and placebo groups. There is no FDA guidance on the use of estradiol (vaginal) in specific gender populations, racial populations, patients with renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. Additionally, there is no FDA guidance on its use during pregnancy, labor and delivery, or in nursing mothers. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established. Estradiol (vaginal) is administered vaginally. The usual dosage form is a cream delivered with a calibrated plastic applicator. The medication should be stored at room temperature and protected from temperatures exceeding 40°C (104°F). It should be kept out of the reach of children. There is limited information regarding the pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of estradiol (vaginal) in the drug label. Serious ill effects have not been reported following acute ingestion of large doses of estrogen-containing drug products by young children. Overdosage may cause nausea and vomiting, and withdrawal bleeding may occur in females.
